title: How to read this specification
summary: Conventions, figures and profiles: what helps to know before you start.

phrase.text: This specification describes the whole PseudoLearn language and its engine, with examples that really run every time it is built.
Everything that belongs to the language looks like code; everything you have to fill in yourself looks like a slot.

title.text: How to read a written form

phrase.text: A written form is the mould of a construct: it says which words are fixed, which slots you fill in and which parts you may leave out.
Figures show what the program text does not: memory, the order in which each part runs and what the engine records.
PseudoLearn has two vocabularies with exactly the same rules: you can program in Spanish or in English and the result is the same.
An edition is a closed version of the language; this specification describes the 2026 edition.

title: Overview
summary: What PseudoLearn is and what happens to a program from the moment you write it until it ends.

phrase.text: PseudoLearn is a pseudocode language that really runs: what you write is analysed, run and can be watched step by step.

title.text: The journey of a program: from text to execution

phrase.text: Before running a program, the engine breaks it into pieces, checks that it makes sense and translates it into simple instructions for its virtual machine.
The engine does three different jobs with a program: analysing it without running it, running it, and letting you observe what happens inside.

title.text: Determinism: the same program always gives the same result

phrase.text: With the same program, the same inputs and the same seed, the engine always produces the same output, on any computer.
Every run ends in one of six states: it finished well, it failed, it is waiting for input, it is waiting for the outside world, it was cancelled or it ran out of a limit.
The engine warns with diagnostics: errors prevent running, warnings do not, and failures happen while the program runs.

title: Lexical structure
summary: The smallest pieces of the text: words, numbers, texts, signs and comments.

phrase.text: A program is UTF-8 text; the engine reads it character by character and remembers the line and column of each one to point at errors precisely.
Spaces, tabs and line breaks only separate pieces: indentation does not change the meaning and a line break does not end a statement.
A comment starts with
and runs to the end of the line; the engine keeps it but does not run it.
An identifier is the name you choose for a variable, a subroutine or a type: it starts with a letter or an underscore and distinguishes upper case, lower case and accents.
Reserved words belong to the language itself, such as
or
; you cannot use them as the name of a variable.
A number written in the program is an integer if it has only digits and a real if it has a point with digits on both sides.
A text goes between double or single quotes; if it contains exactly one character it is a
, and in any other case it is a
Operators and signs are the pieces made of symbols, such as
or
; the engine always reads the longest possible piece.
Every simple statement ends with a semicolon; the words that open and close blocks, such as
or
, do not.
A lexical error appears when a piece of the text does not form any valid token: a character the language does not know, an invented escape or unclosed quotes.

title: Types and values
summary: Which kinds of data exist, how much they hold and how they relate.

phrase.text: Every piece of data has a type that says which values it can hold and what can be done with it; PseudoLearn has five primitive types and every other type is built from them.
A value only moves by itself from one type to another when the target type contains it whole: from
to
, from
to
and from a subclass to its superclass.

title.text: Inference: the type is always declared

phrase.text: In PseudoLearn no variable guesses its type: each one is declared with
and an explicit type before it is used.
An array is a row (or a table) of boxes of the same type, with a fixed size and numbered from zero.
A vector is a list that grows and shrinks while the program runs; all its elements have the same type.
A dictionary stores key-value pairs: you look up by the key and get the value, like in a phone book.
A record groups several named pieces of data into a single value, like a card with its sections; assigning it copies it whole.
An enumeration is a type with a closed list of named values, like the colours of a traffic light.
A variant is a type whose values can take several different shapes, each with its own data, like a figure that can be a circle or a rectangle.
represents a value that may be missing and
an operation that may go well or badly; both force you to look at the bad case before using the value.
A subroutine is also a value: it can be stored in a variable, passed as an argument or returned, and called later.
A generic is a subroutine or a type written once for any type: the concrete type is filled in when it is used.
takes a complete picture of a value and returns it as
: everything can be read, but nobody can change it.
is a sequence of octets, numbers from 0 to 255; it is used to work with binary data, such as the exact content of a file.
The engine checks everything it can before running; whatever depends on concrete values, such as dividing by zero, it checks when running.

title: Expressions and operators
summary: How things are computed: arithmetic, comparisons, logic and the order of operations.

There are three ways of dividing:

Comparison operators ask something about two values and answer with a

When an expression has several operators, precedence decides which applies first:

title: Declarations and statements
summary: Creating variables and constants, giving them values and ending each instruction.

phrase.text: creates variables: named, typed boxes where the program keeps a value that can change.
A
names a value that never changes, and the engine computes it before running.
stores a new value in a variable and forgets the one it had.
A designator is something that names a place where a value can be stored: a variable, an array cell or an attribute of an object.
Before running, the engine walks every possible path of the program and rejects reading a variable that some path has not given a value to.
A variable that is declared and never used, or written and never read, produces a warning: the program works, but something is left over.

title: Control flow
summary: Deciding, repeating, leaving early and leaving clean-up for the end.

while
a condition is true, and checks it before every round, including the first.

until
the condition is true, and always does at least one round.

title: Subroutines
summary: Naming a piece of a program, passing it data and receiving a result.

phrase.text: A subprogram is a named piece of program: it is written once and used as many times as needed.
Parameters are the input variables of a subprogram: on every call they receive a
copy
of the values passed to it.
A
parameter is another name for the caller's variable: whatever the subprogram does to it, it does to that variable.
Calling a subprogram means pausing what you are doing, running the subprogram with its arguments and coming back exactly to where you paused.
ends the subprogram on the spot and, if it has a return type, hands the value to the caller.
Every name exists only inside its
scope
: from where it is declared to the end of the block that contains it.
A recursive subprogram calls itself with a smaller problem, until it reaches a case so simple that it is solved without calling itself.
A
only computes: it does not write, read, or touch files or the network. Whatever has effects is declared with

title: Programs and modules
summary: How a program is organised into units, files and packages.

phrase.text: A program is a text with
a single algorithm
and, around it, the pieces that algorithm uses: subprograms, classes, records, enumerations and constants.
When a program grows, it is split into files: every file is a
module
, and a module uses what another one makes
public
by importing it.

title: Objects
summary: Classes, attributes, methods, inheritance and interfaces.

phrase.text: A class is a mould: it describes what data every object keeps (its
attributes
) and what it can do (its
methods
A method is a subprogram that lives inside a class and works on a particular object: the one named before the dot.
creates an object and runs its constructor, which prepares the attributes before anyone uses it.
With
, a class receives the attributes and methods of another and can change how some of them behave.
An interface is a list of methods a class
promises
to have; it lets you write code that works with any class that keeps the promise.
Assigning an object does not duplicate it: it gives another name to the same object. To get a new object with the same data you need
PseudoLearn deliberately leaves out some pieces of other object languages, and when it recognises them it explains so with a message of its own.

title: Errors and diagnostics
summary: How the engine warns that something is wrong, and why.

phrase.text: A diagnostic is not a sentence: it is a piece of data with a stable code, a class, a severity and a position. The message you read is built afterwards, in your language.
Severity says what to do with a diagnostic: an error prevents running, a warning tells you and lets you continue.
After a syntax error, the engine looks for a safe point to keep reading: that way it reports every independent error at once, each one only once.

title: Concurrency and asynchrony
summary: Several tasks that take turns, talk to each other and wait for the outside world.

phrase.text: A
unit can pause half-way while it waits for something;
marks in the code every point where that pause may happen.
opens a space where tasks that progress together are spawned;
waits for
all
of them to finish, so none is left loose.
A channel is a fixed-capacity queue through which some tasks send values and others receive them, in order and without sharing memory.
To touch the outside world —the console, files, the clock, the network— a program asks for a
capability
: a key that gives access to one single thing.

title: Library
summary: Ready-to-use functions: text, mathematics, files, JSON, network and time.

phrase.text: The library is the set of functions the language brings: each has a fixed identity, a name in each profile and a signature that does not change with the language.
Text functions measure, trim, search and transform strings without ever modifying the original: they always return a new one.
Conversions change a value's type explicitly: from number to text, from text to number, or from real to text with a fixed number of decimals.
Mathematical functions compute roots, logarithms and trigonometry with results exact to the last bit, and rounding functions go from real to integer in four different ways.
PseudoLearn's randomness comes from a source with a
seed
: with the same seed, the program always draws the same numbers.
shows values on the output and
asks the person using the program for values: they are the simplest way to talk to the outside.
To read or write files you ask for a folder capability, open the file with it, and every operation returns a
that may carry an
turns a JSON text into a value you can walk through, and
goes the other way.
With the network capability, a program builds an HTTP request, sends it and receives a response with its status, headers and body.
The clock gives instants in nanoseconds, the timer waits, and
turns an instant into year, month, day and time without depending on the machine.

title: The engine inside
summary: The parts of the engine that analyse, translate and run every program.

phrase.text: The engine processes a program in layers: each one receives the previous result, checks or transforms it and hands it to the next.
Objects, arrays and texts created while running live on the
heap
, and the collector recovers those nobody can reach without the program ever noticing.
Tasks do not really run at the same time: a deterministic
schedule
decides which one advances, and that is why every run always follows the same order.
Everything a program does towards the outside happens in program order and is noted on a
tape
, with which the run can be replayed without touching the world again.
Execution can be watched step by step: the engine emits a
trace
of events, and every event carries what changed in memory.

Limits are resources set by whoever runs the program —depth, statements, memory, time— and are not part of the language: a program that does not reach them gives the same result under any configuration.
A program can also be compiled to a native executable that behaves exactly as in the virtual machine: the same output, the same failures, the same messages.
